newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian govt denies sheltering war crimes suspect.
newsitem.headline: Croatian govt denies sheltering war crimes suspect.

text.p: The Croatian government on Thursday denied reports that a Bosnian Croat wanted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal had lived in a state-owned hotel in the port city of Split for almost a year.

Globus, Croatia's leading independent newspaper, said this week that Ivica Rajic, a militia leader linked to the 1993 massacre of 16 Moslem civilians, had a flat in the hotel owned by the Defence Ministry.

It published pictures purportedly showing Rajic near the hotel last week reading a newspaper. Rajic had since left Croatia, Globus said. United Nations sources said the tribunal, based in The Hague, had been alerted about the report.
Defence Minister Gojko Susak said the Globus story was wrong and he planned to sue the weekly, a strong critic of the nationalist government.
Susak said on state television's evening news that the man in the Globus photographs was an employee of the hotel.
"The Ministry will sue both the weekly and the author of the column," said the defence minister, a Bosnian-born Croat.

"The man on the cover is not Ivica Rajic but Vlatko Perkovic, who is in charge of the maintenance of the central heating system in the Hotel Zagreb (in Split)," the defence ministry said in a separate statement.
"Secondly, Ivica Rajic doesn't live in the Hotel Zagreb or any other building belonging to the Defence Ministry.
"Thirdly, the Ministry is unaware of the whereabouts of this former HVO (Bosnian Croat militia) member," it said.

Last July, Globus published pictures of number one Bosnian Croat war crimes suspect Dario Kordic, former head of the Bosnian wing of Croatia's ruling HDZ party, allegedly living in a defence ministry apartment in Zagreb.
The government did not challenge that report.
Kordic is accused of complicity in massacres and ethnic expulsions of Moslems in the Lasva Valley of central Bosnia.
The U.N. Security Council censured the Croatian government two weeks ago over its failure to arrest and extradite to the tribunal indictees reported to have been seen in Croatia.

Croatia armed Bosnian Croats in their 1993-94 separatist war against the Moslem-led central government. Bosnian Moslems and Croats are now in an uneasy federation held together by U.S. diplomatic pressure.

The tribunal has so far indicted 18 Croats, 54 Serbs and three Moslems for atrocities, most of them in Bosnia's 1992-95 war and the rest in Croatia's sporadic 1991-95 conflict with minority Serbs. It has seven suspects in custody.

The Council of Europe admitted Croatia last week as its 40th member but diplomats said further progress by Zagreb towards European Union integration would depend in part on cooperation with the tribunal.

Under special legislation passed by parliament six months ago Croatia is committed to extraditing indicted war criminals found on its territory. But only one of several indicted suspects spotted on Croatian territory has been handed over.

Foreign Minister Mate Granic told Globus in an interview published parallel to the Rajic article that he did not know of Rajic's whereabouts but said Croatia would act if his presence in Croatia was proven.
